articles.title: Qualidade do ar em Manaus é a pior do Brasil pelo 2º dia seguido | G1
articles.standfirst: Índice de 153 na plataforma IQAir classifica ar da capital como 'insalubre' na manhã desta quarta-feira (25). Sensores do sistema Selva indicam situação crítica em sete municípios do interior.
articles.summary: A qualidade do ar em Manaus atingiu níveis insalubres nesta quarta-feira (25), enquanto a seca histórica coloca 54 municípios do Amazonas em situação de emergência.
articles.body:
Manaus registra pior qualidade do ar no Brasil nesta quarta-feira (25) — Foto: Lucas Macedo/g1

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Manaus voltou a registrar a pior qualidade do ar entre as capitais e principais cidades monitoradas do Brasil na manhã desta quarta-feira (25), marcando o segundo dia consecutivo no topo do ranking nacional . O índice de 153 na escala AQI classificou o ar da capital como "insalubre" na plataforma internacional IQAir.

O levantamento da plataforma considera as medições de três estações instaladas na cidade e aponta o material particulado fino (PM2.5) como o principal poluente, com concentração média de 58,3 µg/m³ às 5h.

Já no monitoramento local do Sistema Eletrônico de Vigilância Ambiental (Selva), desenvolvido pela Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA), a maior parte dos sensores espalhados pelos bairros de Manaus indicava qualidade do ar entre "ruim" e "muito ruim" nas primeiras horas do dia.

Os maiores índices de concentração de poluentes registrados pelos sensores do Selva na capital ocorriam nas zonas Leste, Sul e Centro-Sul, com destaque para os pontos monitorados no Zumbi dos Palmares e Armando Mendes (97,3 µg/m³), Aleixo e Coroado (79,5 µg/m³), Distrito Industrial I e Crespo (79,2 µg/m³), Morro da Liberdade (75,2 µg/m³) e Petrópolis (73,1 µg/m³).

🔎 A qualidade do ar é considerada boa pelo sistema Selva quando a concentração de partículas fica entre 0 e 25 µg/m³. Acima desse valor, a classificação varia de moderada a péssima, conforme a quantidade de poluentes no ar.

Interior do Amazonas tem índices ainda mais críticos

O impacto da fumaça também atinge municípios da Região Metropolitana e do interior do estado. Segundo o mapa de monitoramento do Selva, sete cidades apresentavam índices classificados no nível "péssimo", acima de 160 µg/m³, na manhã desta quarta-feira.

Urucará : 205,8 µg/m³ Maués: 196,5 µg/m³

Outros municípios próximos também registravam alteração na qualidade do ar pelo sistema da UEA, como Itapiranga , com 101,1 µg/m³ nível "muito ruim", e Boa Vista do Ramos , com 62,7 µg/m³ (nível "ruim").

Orientações para população se proteger da fumaça

A Defesa Civil de Manaus orienta a população a manter a hidratação, evitar atividades físicas ao ar livre, usar máscara PFF2 em caso de exposição à fumaça e acompanhar os alertas oficiais. Crianças, idosos, gestantes e pessoas com doenças respiratórias devem redobrar os cuidados.

A exposição à fumaça pode provocar tosse, falta de ar, irritação nos olhos e outros sintomas respiratórios.

Seca deixa 54 municípios em situação de emergência

O agravamento das queimadas e da poluição atmosférica ocorre em meio à forte estiagem que atinge o Amazonas. Segundo o boletim mais recente da Defesa Civil do estado, o número de municípios em situação de emergência por conta da seca subiu de 52 para 54, o equivalente a quase 90% das cidades amazonenses.

Ao todo, quase 170 mil famílias, mais de 670 mil pessoas, já foram afetadas pela vazante dos rios em todo o estado. Com a redução drástica no nível das águas, comunidades ficam isoladas e enfrentam dificuldades para o transporte de alimentos, água potável e combustíveis, cenário que também favorece a propagação de focos de incêndio na região.

articles.title: Veja 15 cidades do interior de SP que ganharam repercussão nacional | G1
articles.standfirst: Pioneirismo, ciência, curiosidades e até uma cidade que ficou famosa por alguns minutos: para celebrar os 15 anos das páginas locais do g1 nas áreas de cobertura da TV TEM, especial reúne acontecimentos marcantes de municípios das regiões de Bauru, Rio Preto, Sorocaba, Itapetininga e Presidente Prudente.
articles.summary: Em especial de 15 anos, relembramos fatos marcantes em cidades do interior de SP, desde adoção pioneira e tecnologia nuclear até memes e casos de grande repercussão.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma descoberta científica capaz de chamar a atenção do país inteiro, memes de carnaval, dialetos próprios, projetos pioneiros e personagens que saíram do anonimato e viraram fenômeno nacional: um acontecimento é suficiente para colocar uma pequena cidade no mapa do Brasil.

Nesta quarta-feira (25), as páginas nas regiões de Bauru e Marília , Itapetininga e região, São José do Rio Preto e Araçatuba e Sorocaba e Jundiaí debutam e completam 15 anos no ar .

O marco inicial da cobertura local foi em 25 de novembro de 2011, quando os sites regionais nas áreas de cobertura da TV TEM , afiliada da Rede Globo, entraram no ar, como parte do projeto de expansão do portal iniciado em 2010. Mais recentemente, em 31 de agosto de 2025, Presidente Prudente também passou a contar com uma página local, ampliando a presença do g1 no interior paulista.

15 anos g1 TV TEM: relembre 15 cidades do interior de SP que ganharam repercussão nacional — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

🎂 Para celebrar os 15 anos do g1 no interior paulista, o aniversariante ganha uma retrospectiva à altura de um debutante: 15 fatos marcantes que colocaram a região nos holofotes nacionais. Entre eles, histórias que fizeram até uma cidade com apenas 907 habitantes conquistar seus 15 minutos de fama. Confira abaixo:

Veja os fatos que colocaram as cidades da área de cobertura do g1 da TV TEM em destaque nacional — Foto: Arte/g1

📍Região de São José do Rio Preto e Araçatuba

Foto de Monsenhor Ângelo Angioni à esquerda; Dorival Júnior e Vasco Pedro da Gama Filho com Teodora em Catanduva (SP) ao centro; reféns sendo usados de escudo humano em cima de carro em Araçatuba à direita — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

José Bonifácio — Caminho para a canonização: Desde 2008, José Bonifácio ganhou destaque com internacional com Monsenhor Ângelo Angioni, um pároco que dedicou décadas de sua vida religiosa ao município, avançando em seu processo de canonização. Em 2015, equipes de Roma vieram para a cidade fazer a exumação do corpo dele e, à época, o seu coração estava intacto , o que chamou a atenção da comunidade católica e do país inteiro. Em outubro de 2025, o Vaticano concedeu o título de "venerável" ao religioso. Ele fundou igrejas, capelas, casas de retiro, residências religiosas, espaços para idosos e para atividades paroquiais.

Catanduva — Marco histórico na adoção: O município do interior de SP foi o lar do primeiro casal gay a conseguir adotar judicialmente uma criança no Brasi l, em 2006. Dorival Pereira de Carvalho Júnior e Vasco Pedro da Gama Filho fizeram história ao adotar a pequena Theodora, então com quatro anos. Passados quatro anos, eles adotaram Helena e descobriram, durante o processo, que as duas eram irmãs biológicas.

Araçatuba — Mega assalto : Em agosto de 2021, a cidade chocou o país após uma quadrilha de 30 criminosos fortemente armados atacarem agências bancárias no centro , usar explosivos e fazer moradores reféns como escudos humanos . Na ocasião , foram utilizados carros blindados e adaptados para carregar armamento de guerra pesado, capaz de derrubar até um helicóptero. Três pessoas morreram na ação e outras cinco ficaram feridas, incluindo um jovem que teve os pés amputados. Conforme a Justiça Federal, o prejuízo do roubo às agências bancárias chegou a R$ 17 milhões.

Região aérea de Borá (SP) à esquerda; Ministro da Saúde aplicando vacina contra Covid em moradora de Botucatu (SP) durante a pandemia ao centro; à direita, prainha de Sabino (SP). — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Borá — A ex-menor cidade do Brasil: Desmembrada de Paraguaçu Paulista em 1964 e batizada em homenagem a uma abelha comum na região no início do século 20, Borá tem apenas 32 ruas e nenhum semáforo. O município ocupou o posto de cidade menos populosa do Brasil a partir do Censo de 1991 (quando tinha 751 habitantes), perdendo o título apenas em 2013 para Serra da Saudade (MG), ao chegar a 834 moradores impulsionada pela oferta de empregos e pelo sossego.

Botucatu — Modelo para todo o país : Em 2021, o município ganhou destaque ao participar de uma pesquisa inédita de vacinação em massa contra a Covid-19 , que avaliou a efetividade da imunização em larga escala na população adulta, de 18 a 60 anos, moradora da cidade. Um esquema grandioso foi montado para vacinar esse público-alvo em poucos dias. A primeira dose foi aplicada em maio de 2021 e a segunda dose em agosto do mesmo ano. Toda a pesquisa custou R$ 11 milhões , que foram financiados pelo Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq).

Sabino — Dialeto próprio: A pequena cidade de pouco mais de 5 mil habitantes ganhou projeção nacional, com direito a reportagem no Jornal Nacional, pela forma peculiar de comunicação de seus moradores, que desenvolveram um dialeto próprio repleto de expressões locais . O "sabinês" consiste em falar as palavras de trás para a frente , movendo a posição das sílabas. Embora a origem seja incerta, acredita-se que o dialeto tenha surgido como uma brincadeira entre amigos na década de 1950.

Pastilhas de urânio que são usadas no submarino de Iperó à esquerda; Juliana Muniz no pole dance ao centro; o cão-guia Café à direita — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Iperó — Tecnologia nuclear: No Centro Industrial Nuclear de Aramar, em Iperó (SP), são desenvolvidas tecnologias relacionadas à geração de energia elétrica por fonte nuclear . Um dos projetos é do reator nuclear que vai equipar o primeiro submarino brasileiro com propulsão nuclear , projeto estratégico de defesa nacional. A previsão de entrega é para o ano de 2033.

São Roque — Superação no pole dance : A cidade foi cenário da história da empresária Juliana Muniz, que ganhou destaque nacional e até medalhas internacionais ao mostrar como encontrou no pole dance uma ferramenta de transformação pessoal , autoestima e superação.

Salto de Pirapora — Cão-guia e tutora : O município emocionou o país com a história de parceria e independência entre a jovem Maria Stockler Carvalhosa e seu cão-guia, Café. Depois de perder a visão aos 13 anos por causa de um tumor cerebral, ela encontrou autonomia graças ao trabalho da maior escola de cães-guia da América Latina, instituição sem fins lucrativos sediada na cidade. A partir do 'match', Maria teve autonomia para abrir uma editora especializada em audiolivros, onde trabalha como curadora.

Acidente em Taguaí (SP) à esquerda; entrada de Laranjal Paulista (SP) ao centro; Ione Lao do meme 'Cidade Maldita' em Itapetininga (à direita) — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Taguaí — Tragédia na rodovia: Em novembro de 2020, o município foi palco de um dos mais graves acidentes rodoviários do estado de São Paulo, considerado o mais fatal em 22 anos à época dos fatos, quando a colisão entre um ônibus que transportava trabalhadores e um caminhão provocou 42 mortes na Rodovia Alfredo de Oliveira Carvalho.

Laranjal Paulista — Capital dos brinquedos: Com produção estimada em cerca de 60 milhões de brinquedos por ano , a cidade se consolidou como um dos maiores polos do setor no país, atraindo inclusive turistas interessados em visitar as lojas e fábricas locais. A representação foi tanta que até mesmo a entrada do município faz alusão aos brinquedos.

Itapetininga — " Cidade Maldita" : Há 15 anos, o município viralizou em todo o Brasil e ganhou o apelido bem-humorado de "cidade maldita" durante o feriado de carnaval, em um meme que atravessou gerações nas redes sociais. A resposta de Ione Lao foi dita ao repórter Nohlan Hubertus, durante uma entrevista a uma emissora. O material não chegou a ir ao ar na televisão, mas foi publicado em seu canal pessoal no YouTube e gerou milhões de visualizações. O g1 entrou em contato com a professora para uma entrevista, mas Ione preferiu não comentar sobre o assunto.

Rede urbana de gás biometano em Presidente Prudente (SP) à esquerda; fotografia vencedora do concurso de pôr do sol mais bonito do país em Sabino (SP) ao centro; Deolane Bezerra (à direita) — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Presidente Epitácio — O pôr do sol mais bonito do Brasil: Banhada pelo Rio Paraná, a estância turística venceu a disputa nacional promovida pelo Fantástico com uma foto clicada na orla pelo morador Carlos Rayzaro. A imagem foi vencedora disputando com outras cinco fotografias de outros estados do país, e mostra o sol se pondo atrás da ponte que liga São Paulo a Mato Grosso do Sul, um cartão-postal da região.

Presidente Prudente — Pioneirismo no biometano: Em novembro de 2025, o município tornou-se pioneiro ao inaugurar uma rede urbana abastecida por biometano produzido a partir de resíduos da cana-de-açúcar, apostando em energia limpa e sustentável. Segundo a Agência Reguladora de Serviços Públicos do Estado de São Paulo (Arsesp), o projeto leva gás canalizado e opera de forma independente. O gás é distribuído pela Necta, com produção da Usina Cocal, localizada em Narandiba (SP).

Tupi Paulista — Destino de Deolane Bezerra: A penitenciária feminina da cidade foi questionada ao receber a advogada e influenciadora digital Deolane Bezerra , presa por suspeita de participação em um esquema de lavagem de dinheiro ligado ao PCC , levantando o debate sobre os critérios que a levaram para o interior paulista em vez de Tremembé , conhecido como o "presídio dos famosos". Até a última atualização desta reportagem, ela segue presa desde o dia 21 de maio.

articles.summary: Mega-Sena 3090 premia aposta de Junqueiro com R$ 38 mil na quina e acumula prêmio de R$ 75 milhões; confira os números sorteados e ganhadores em Alagoas.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma aposta feita em Junqueiro acertou, na terça-feira (24), cinco dos seis números sorteados no concurso da 3090 da Mega-Sena, realizado em São Paulo. O jogo vencedor faturou o prêmio de R$ 38.160,32.

Nenhum apostador acertou os seis números e o prêmio principal acumulou em R$ 75 milhões. O próximo sorteio acontece na quinta-feira (26).

Os números sorteados foram: 10 - 14 - 27 - 28 - 47 - 57.

Em Alagoas, além da quina, outras 23 apostas acertaram quatro números durante o sorteio. Os apostadores ganharam R$ 588 e R$ 3.528 (confira abaixo) .

g1 transmite sorteios das Loterias Caixa

Bilhetes da Mega-Sena, em imagem de arquivo — Foto: Marcelo Brandt/G1

O g1 passou a transmitir todos os sorteios das Loterias Caixa, ao vivo. A transmissão começa momentos antes de cada dia de concursos, no site e no canal do g1 no YouTube.

A Mega-Sena realiza três sorteios por semana: às terças, quintas e sábados, sempre às 21h.

As apostas podem ser feitas em qualquer casa lotérica do país ou pela internet, por meio da internet banking da Caixa Econômica Federal, além do site ou aplicativo das Loterias Caixa, acessíveis por celular, computador ou tablet. Para participar, é necessário ter mais de 18 anos.

A aposta mínima, com seis números, custa R$ 6. Quanto mais números forem marcados, maior será o valor da aposta e as chances de ganhar.

Resultado do concurso 3090 da Mega-Sena. — Foto: Reprodução/Caixa

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e do tipo de aposta realizada.

Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860, segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00, a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292, ainda de acordo com a instituição.

articles.title: Manicure morta em Praia Grande fugiu de ex-companheiro agressor | G1
articles.standfirst: Beatriz Borges Monteiro de Castro, de 20 anos, havia solicitado medida protetiva contra o ex-companheiro em Diadema (SP), após episódios de agressão e ameaças de morte. Ela se mudou para Praia Grande (SP) há cerca de um ano.
articles.summary: Beatriz Borges Monteiro de Castro foi vítima de feminicídio em Praia Grande; o atual companheiro, Celso Miranda de Souza Junior, foi preso após se entregar à polícia.
articles.body:
Beatriz Borges Monteiro de Castro foi encontrada morta em Praia Grande — Foto: Redes sociais

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Beatriz Borges Monteiro de Castro, a manicure de 20 anos encontrada morta com sinais de violência na casa onde vivia com o companheiro , Celso Miranda de Souza Junior, havia se mudado para Praia Grande , no litoral de São Paulo, para se afastar de outro relacionamento marcado por agressões e ameaças de morte .

Antes de se mudar para a Baixada Santista com a mãe, Beatriz morava em Diadema (SP), onde teria sido agredida e ameaçada de morte pelo ex-companheiro. Segundo apurado pelo g1 , a jovem chegou a solicitar uma medida protetiva contra o homem para evitar novos episódios de violência.

A manicure foi encontrada morta na madrugada de sábado (21), no bairro Jardim Princesa, em Praia Grande. O atestado de óbito apontou asfixia como causa da morte . O companheiro dela, Celso Miranda, foi preso pelo crime após se apresentar à polícia neste domingo (22).

Conforme apurado pelo g1 junto a uma familiar de Beatriz, a jovem havia se mudado para Praia Grande há cerca de um ano para evitar contato com o ex-companheiro, que teria a agredido durante a gravidez.

O relacionamento entre os dois durou aproximadamente quatro anos. Durante esse período, segundo o relato, o homem apresentava comportamento agressivo: além de agredir Beatriz fisicamente, quebrava pertences dela e praticava violência psicológica, afastando-a da família e dos amigos.

Beatriz decidiu terminar o relacionamento após sofrer agressões durante a gestação. Cerca de dez dias depois do nascimento da criança, porém, o homem a procurou dizendo que queria ver a criança e se recusou a ir embora.

Beatriz Borges Monteiro de Castro e Celso Miranda de Souza Junior — Foto: Reprodução

Diante da situação, a jovem teria sido agredida novamente pelo ex-companheiro e decidiu deixar a cidade. O homem não tem envolvimento com a morte de Beatriz.

Procurada, a Secretaria de Segurança Pública de São Paulo (SSP-SP) não se manifestou até a última atualização desta reportagem. O g1 não localizou a defesa do ex-companheiro de Beatriz acusado de violência.

A Justiça decretou a prisão preventiva de Celso Miranda de Souza Junior, o atual companheiro de Beatriz, e apontou a saída do local antes da chegada da polícia como um dos motivos para a decisão. O investigado se apresentou espontaneamente neste domingo (22).

A advogada Luciene Ribeiro de Castilhos afirma que tentava organizar a apresentação de Celso desde as 11h de sábado (21), antes do decreto de prisão, às 13h17. Ela contesta que ele tenha fugido para evitar as autoridades.

A advogada solicitou a revogação da medida ou sua substituição por medidas cautelares. A defesa alega que o investigado é primário, tem bons antecedentes, residência fixa e não possui histórico de violência em relacionamentos anteriores.

A defesa também questionou a existência de elementos nos autos para apontar que ele teve a intenção de matar Beatriz, questionando o enquadramento do crime como feminicídio qualificado.

articles.title: My family died in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated
articles.summary: BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in the war.
articles.body:
I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground .

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.

With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.

He said he did not know anything about who killed them.

"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

articles.title: Russia's own figures show it has lost almost 500,000 people in Ukraine war
articles.summary: Leaked data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia.
articles.body:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.

BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.

Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.

The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.

During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.

Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.

Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

How we came to a figure near half a million

The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.

We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.

Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.

Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).

Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.

In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.

At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.

This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.

The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.

The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.

In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.

In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

articles.title: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
articles.summary: Sunday’s election could see a far-right party enter the Spanish government for first time.
articles.body:
Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments.

"What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei.

"If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said Sánchez.

He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy.

In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister.

His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image.

Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left.

Yet in Spain, Sánchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal.

In a bullring in Valencia, the same day that Sánchez was staging his rally, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo told supporters that the last few years of Socialist-led government had been "insulting and even humiliating for a lot of people". He added: "We know them, they are capable of anything."

A couple of days earlier, Ignacio Garriga, spokesman for Vox, had gone further, describing Sánchez as "a very dangerous psychopath".

Both the PP and Vox have cast doubt on the neutrality of postal votes and votes cast by Spaniards abroad ahead of the election, suggesting that government manipulation could sway them in its favour.

"This is a campaign that is overwhelmingly ideological," said Cristina Monge, a political scientist at the Complutense University. "That means that it is not so much about voters rewarding or punishing a government's performance or the proposals being made, but about belonging to one or other ideological bloc."

Much of the hostility to Sánchez stems from his reliance on hard-left and separatist parties.

Ahead of the 2023 general election, he faced fierce criticism from the right for his reliance on the pro-independence EH Bildu coalition, which had links to the defunct Basque armed group ETA.

After that vote, he was able to form a new administration with the support of another separatist party, Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for an amnesty for all Catalans facing legal action for their role in a failed 2017 bid for independence.

At the time, Núñez Feijóo accused Sánchez of being "a prime minister who has bought his investiture in exchange for the judicial impunity of his partners".

Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Carlos III University, said those parliamentary partnerships "fed the rhetoric of the right and far right, which was that Pedro Sánchez is an amoral person without scruples – someone whose word can't be trusted and who just wants to remain in power".

This legislation has been one of turmoil for Sánchez, during which he has been unable to push a single budget through parliament.

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

In addition, the prime minister has been corralled by a litany of judicial investigations. He has acknowledged errors of judgement in trusting two close former associates in the Socialist Party, José Luis Ábalos, who has been given a 24-year-jail sentence for corruption-related crimes, and Santos Cerdán, who is due to go on trial on similar charges.

By contrast, he has defended his former attorney general, Álvaro García Ortiz, who was barred from public office for revealing confidential information, and his brother, David, who was barred from office for nine years after being found guilty of irregularities in taking on a post as a regional arts director.

In the most controversial case, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial for influence peddling.

She denies wrongdoing and Sánchez has said the cases involving García Ortiz, his brother and wife are "nasty politics, not corruption", blaming them on efforts by his political opponents to use the judiciary to destabilise his government.

Politicians on the right draw no such distinction between the various cases, and Vox leader Santiago Abascal describes the government as "a criminal mafia".

María Pérez, a young office worker who has no political allegiance, says she is going to vote for the PP, partly because of her concerns about the country's housing crisis and the rail system, which has seen two major tragedies this year, but above all due to the judicial investigations.

"I think that Sánchez has lost credibility with all the corruption cases," she says. "It seems that everyone in government is involved… so I'm not sure I want them to continue governing. I believe it's time for a change."

Allegations that Sánchez has co-opted state institutions, such as the CIS national research centre, which publishes opinion polls, and national broadcaster RTVE, have only compounded the right's view of him as a populist who has scant regard for the rule of law.

However, with the far right seemingly set to enter government for the first time in Spain's democratic era, claims of demagoguery cut both ways.

Politicians on the left say that coalition administrations formed by the PP and Vox in four of Spain's 17 regions are a blueprint for socially regressive policies they plan to implement on a national level after the election.

In all four of those regions, Vox has negotiated the introduction of "national priority", which seeks to give Spaniards priority access to public services and subsidies ahead of foreigners.

The Castilla y León region has also seen culture-related controversies driven by Vox. Most recently, a play about left-wing poet and dramatist Federico García Lorca, who was killed by right-wing rebels during the 1936-39 civil war, was cancelled in the region's capital, Valladolid, apparently at the behest of the Vox-controlled local culture ministry.

Last month the same department published new guidelines governing the awarding of subsidies for films, stating that projects involving what it called "ideological indoctrination" would not be eligible. Spain's culture minister, Ernest Urtasun, described this as "an intolerable attempt at censorship".

Susana Fuertes, a schoolteacher who will vote for the left on Sunday, said such moves are a sinister throwback to the dictatorship of Francisco Franco.

"These political messages take us back to the Franco era by talking about getting rid of basic civil rights regarding women, gender equality and immigration," she said. "All of this has been said in such an aggressive tone, with insults and lack of respect for people who don't share the same ideas."

Critics of Núñez Feijóo argue that he has already shown signs of taking on Vox's agenda by hardening his rhetoric on immigration and promising to roll back a law allowing euthanasia and eliminate the equality ministry, which manages matters related to gender, sexuality and ethnicity.

Spain's deep left-right schism has also been visible beyond the political arena.

Hooded anti-fascist youths have clashed with police on a number of occasions on the campaign trail, such as when they demonstrated against an appearance by Vox's Abascal in A Coruña.

An arguably more visible phenomenon has been far-right youths. In one incident, several dozen of them raised their arms in the fascist salute and sang the pro-Franco anthem Cara al Sol (Facing the sun) while facing off against housing protesters in Madrid.

A 2025 CIS poll found that around one in five under-25s had a positive view of the dictatorship.

articles.title: British billionaire Sir Chris Hohn directs $551 million to children's causes as his foundation CIFF approves $1.45 billion in charitable investments and reports over $4 billion in active programmes
articles.summary: CIFF, the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, approved $ 1.45 billion in charitable investments in 2025, according to its Annual Report 2025.
articles.body: CIFF, the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, approved $ 1.45 billion in charitable investments in 2025, according to its Annual Report 2025. The report states that $ 901 million of that total came from the foundation's endowment and $ 551 million came from donations from its founder and chair, Sir Chris Hohn, for specific programmes. The foundation's Financial Review describes the same $ 551 million as restricted grants from TCI Fund Management Limited, which the notes say Sir Christopher Hohn ultimately controls. The 2024 figure for that share was $ 328 million, against a total of $ 923 million. CIFF now has over $ 4 billion in active multi-year investments.CIFF receives $551 million from Sir Chris Hohn for children's programmesAccording to the "2025 by the Numbers" section of CIFF's Annual Report 2025, the foundation's approved charitable investments in 2025 totalled $ 1.45 billion. The report says $ 901 million of that total came from CIFF's endowment and $ 551 million came from donations from Sir Chris Hohn for specific programmes. The foundation's Section 172(1) statement gives the same total and states that the 2024 figure was $ 923 million.The same statement gives a 2024 comparison for the Hohn-linked share. It reports that $ 551 million "reflected restricted grants" for specific programmes, against $ 328 million in 2024. CIFF's chief executive, Kate Hampton, repeats the split in her letter in the report. She writes that charitable commitments rose to over $ 1.45 billion, with $ 551 million coming from restricted commitments from Sir Chris Hohn.TCI Fund Management donates $481 million to CIFFThe CEO's letter and the "2025 by the Numbers" page describe the $ 551 million as coming from Sir Chris Hohn. The Financial Review in the Section 172(1) statement describes the same figure as restricted grants from TCI Fund Management Limited for specific programmes. The notes to the financial statements say TCI Fund Management Limited, and its group entities, are ultimately controlled by Sir Christopher Hohn, a member and trustee of CIFF.The notes also give the donation details. According to the related-party disclosures, TCI Fund Management Limited made restricted donations of $ 481,002k during 2025, against $ 56,077k in 2024. The notes add that, as at 31 December 2025, it had committed additional restricted funding of $ 189,779k to be paid in future years, against $ 306,622k a year earlier. The same notes record that the CH Foundation (UK), which Sir Christopher founded, made restricted donations of $ 1,456k in 2025.CIFF reports $894 million in income and $574 million in grant paymentsThe foundation received $ 894 million of income in 2025, against $ 304 million in 2024. Of that, $ 802 million came from restricted and unrestricted donations and $ 91 million from investment income, including dividend, interest and rental income from investment properties. The report states that TCI Fund Management Limited also made a $ 320 million unrestricted donation in support of implementation of the 2025–26 business plan. The notes give the 2024 figure for unrestricted donations as $ 160,000k.The report separates commitments from cash paid out. It states that the foundation committed $ 600 million to charitable activities in 2025, against $ 640 million in 2024. That figure consisted of $ 535 million of charitable grant expenditure, $ 6 million of activities undertaken directly and $ 59 million of operating costs. CIFF made $ 574 million of charitable grant payments in 2025, against $ 631 million in 2024. The report says this was the first year of CIFF's shift to a two-year business plan, and that annual disbursements will fluctuate from year to year.CIFF's $8 billion endowment and $4 billion active investment portfolioCIFF's website explains the funding relationship on its "Our story" page. According to that page, Sir Chris Hohn gifted CIFF an endowment in 2002 from his hedge fund, The Children's Investment Fund (TCI), which was founded in the same year. The page says the endowment is now held separately from TCI and that CIFF is an independent organisation. It adds that the endowment continues to be managed by TCI, and that Sir Chris and TCI continue to make gifts that support it. Approved CIFF programmes are funded from the endowment and, in some cases, from restricted gifts from Sir Chris and TCI.The Annual Report puts the endowment's size at the end of 2025 at $ 8.0 billion, after charitable expenditure. According to the report, CIFF now has over $ 4 billion in active multi-year investments. In his founder's letter, dated 9 June 2026, Sir Chris writes that CIFF committed $ 1.45 billion last year to initiatives focused on climate action, health and nutrition, and opportunity and choice for women and girls. articles.title: UK weather: Will there be a White Christmas this year?
articles.summary: It is just a month until the big day but what do the early signs say about the chances of a white Christmas in the UK?
articles.body:
Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?

The likelihood is actually higher than you might imagine.

Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.

Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.

It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.

Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.

The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.

Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.

Are there signs we could have a white Christmas in the UK this year?

A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.

A major one is the record-breaking El Niño which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El Niño's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

In the UK, the impacts tend to be subtle and unreliable.

Strong El Niño events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El Niños is decidedly mixed.

And this is far from the only factor driving our weather.

Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?

Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?

Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.

This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.

Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office , external , taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.

When will we know for sure if Christmas will be white?

It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.

Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.

It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.

You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app .

Share your memories of white Christmas periods. What weather changes have you noticed over time?

articles.title: JeM commander acknowledges terror network in Rawalakot

articles.body: In a significant admission exposing the nexus between terror outfits and Pakistani establishment, Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) commander Masood Ilyas Kashmiri has publicly acknowledged the presence of his group’s armed terrorist network in Rawalakot in POK while alleging state authorities plan to target leaders of an ongoing regional protest movement.Addressing a gathering in Islamabad, Ilyas also criticised Pakistan’s security and intelligence agencies, questioning their failure to identify individuals allegedly involved in anti-state activities as well as those accused of killing paramilitary Pakistan Rangers personnel during recent clashes.The JeM commander went on to say that some of his group’s armed cadres belong to the same local communities that are participating in demonstrations being organised by Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a civil society coalition that has led prolonged protests over economic grievances and governance in the region.He said he had also met with Pakistani govt and security officials in Islamabad to clarify JeM’s position on the unrest. During his address, he alleged officials in Pakistan’s leadership had decided to eliminate both the leaders of the action committee and chief demonstrators in Rawalakot.Ilyas previously drew attention in Sept 2025 when he was seen in a video addressing a gathering in Balakot and acknowledging significant losses suffered by JeM during Indian military strikes on May 7 that year under Operation Sindoor.More than 150 people have died in the protests against Pakistani govt in Rawalakot in the last few months. articles.title: DOJ Announces Largest Anti-Scam Surge in History
articles.summary: DOJ Announces Largest Anti-Scam Surge in US History
articles.body:
The Department of Justice on Tuesday announced the results of what it said was the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in U.S. history, involving more than 400 cases and more than 800 defendants.

"We are identifying and prosecuting criminals who have deceptively and maliciously stolen from Americans of every age and income bracket across the country," Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a news conference . His remarks aired live on Newsmax and the free Newsmax2 streaming platform.

"This protection has included filing over 400 cases in 85 federal districts, with over 800 defendants who have been charged, extradited, pleaded guilty, and some of them sentenced," Blanche said. "We have recovered over $8 billion in intended loss to victims.

"This is the largest anti-scam enforcement surge in history."

The enforcement surge followed an executive order President Donald Trump issued March 6 directing a government-wide crackdown on fraud and predatory schemes targeting Americans.

A. Tysen Duva, assistant attorney general for the DOJ's Criminal Division, said the department had launched investigations targeting criminals in all 50 states and in countries around the world.

"We're not just going after individual scammers," Blanche said. "We are dismantling the criminal networks that have been stealing from the American people for far too long."

FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency has seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds and taken control of more than 14,000 digital devices under Operation Blackout, its global effort to dismantle scam centers.

"We have disrupted, dismantled, and literally leveled 29 scam compounds on four separate continents," Patel said. "These are literal towns where they force people into forced labor, traffic them and then have them perpetrate this illicit activity against the American people."

Patel said the FBI's efforts have helped free more than 2,200 human trafficking victims.

He said the effort also is focused on prevention. Through Operation Level Up, the FBI has prevented nearly $700 million in potential losses among approximately 11,000 people targeted by scammers. Patel said 77% of those individuals were unaware they were being scammed.

More than $143 million in potential losses has been prevented since Trump issued his executive order, according to the DOJ.

"The great news about Operation Level Up is that money never left their bank accounts," Patel said. "They were not scammed. Through our offensive and proactive approach, we prevented 11,000 Americans from being scammed. Behind every one of these scam centers is individuals who are targeted based on their retirement accounts, their kids' college educations, their life savings."

Blanche cited a Gallup poll released in June that found 10% of U.S. adults said they or someone in their household had been scammed last year. Gallup estimated that Americans lost $68 billion to scams in 2025 alone.

Among the schemes targeted in the enforcement surge were jury duty scams originating in Georgia prisons. The DOJ said 14 people were charged in connection with the scams and another 17 were charged in a scheme to smuggle contraband cellphones into Georgia prisons.

Ryan Raybould, the U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Texas, discussed one such case involving three defendants indicted last week on wire fraud and money laundering charges. The defendants, who were in prison or on parole, allegedly used contraband cellphones to falsely tell victims, including some in his district, that they had missed jury duty and would be arrested if they failed to pay a "fine."

Raybould said the defendants "did not need a weapon to target their victims."

"Victims, many of whom are elderly, were told that warrants had been issued for their arrest," Raybould said. "They were instructed to stay on the phone, avoid speaking with anyone or law enforcement, withdraw their money immediately, and deposit their hard-earned life savings in some instances into cryptocurrency kiosks."

"As alleged, this scheme generated approximately $1 million in fraud and victimized hundreds of people across the country."

Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale said investigators identified one victim of jury duty fraud who lost more than $40,000 in personal savings.

"Courts do not demand payment by cryptocurrency to avoid arrest. Law enforcement agencies do not direct citizens to Bitcoin kiosks," Raybould said.

"A few moments of caution can save your life savings."

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
articles.summary: Ábrego García's deportation to El Salvador and return to the US became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
articles.body:
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, has left the US for Spain.

He took a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.

His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.

Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."

In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.

"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."

The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.

For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.

Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.

After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.

At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

articles.body: An Australian family was shocked to discover a five-foot venomous red-bellied black snake emerging from their toilet after it squeezed its way through a narrow sewerage pipe. The 1.5-metre reptile had travelled through a pipe measuring just 50mm in diameter before appearing in the bathroom of a home in Rossmore, southwest Sydney. The family called local snake catcher Daniel May to remove the unexpected visitor. However, the rescue proved unlike anything he had experienced in his career. In an interview with 7News, Daniel May, a professional snake catcher, described the incident as “pretty phenomenal”, revealing that the snake was in such poor condition that he took it into his care.Snake catcher stunned by giant snake found in Australian toiletMay told 7NEWS the snake was unusually large and strong enough to travel through a pipe measuring around 50mm in diameter. Describing the incident, he said: “It was quite a big, chunky and strong snake; even the pipe he swam up was only about 50mm wide so you got to think it was a pretty tight squeeze for him to get up through there and make his way into the toilet.”He also described the unusual rescue as “pretty phenomenal”. According to May, the family was surprised when the snake appeared in the toilet bowl. He suggested they had been trying to chase it away before realising where it had emerged.Australian snake catcher nurses exhausted toilet snake back to healthDespite years of attending calls to remove snakes and other reptiles from homes and businesses across Sydney, May said he had never personally dealt with a similar incident before. Although he had heard of snakes entering toilets in other areas, this was the first time he had encountered one during a rescue.“I’ve seen people post about it. You hear about it a lot in the country and stuff like that ... but that’s the first time, myself, that I’ve had it happen,” he told 7NEWS.The snake was in poor condition after travelling through the sewerage pipe. May said it appeared to be seriously affected by the journey and “looked like it was going to die”. Rather than immediately relocating it, he decided to take it into his care until it had recovered sufficiently to be released.May and his wife monitored the red-bellied black snake over the following couple of days, checking that it was not injured and had regained its strength. They planned to release it on Wednesday, October 21, after allowing it time to recover.Snake catcher warns Sydney residents as snake calls surgeMay also warned that snake encounters were becoming more frequent across Sydney as temperatures began to rise ahead of summer. He said he was receiving as many as six calls a day to catch and remove snakes, with that number expected to reach 10 calls daily in the following weeks.He explained that snakes emerge from their winter hibernation and enter their breeding season, making them more active as they search for mates. “They do a lot more travelling this time of year,” May said, adding that they also ventured through backyards more frequently than usual.You use AI every day. articles.title: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.summary: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former fighter pilot, is the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
articles.body:
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.

Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.

Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".

The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".

While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.

They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.

Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.

The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.

The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.

China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.

For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.

Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

articles.title: Pete Edochie: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor dies aged 79
articles.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
articles.body:
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.

Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.

"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor; he was an institution," Mbah said.

The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.

Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.

He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

articles.title: China: Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.summary: Chen Jining's fall is part of the widest purge in the party's Politburo in several decades.
articles.body:
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.

Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.

Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.

As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.

Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.

While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.

"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.

Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.

The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.

Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.

As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024.

Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus.

Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London.

Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party.

Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown.

Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty.

Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee.

Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down.

Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party.

The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".
