articles.title: Racism, misogyny and homophobia remain in Met force, report finds
articles.summary: A new report has found institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still exist in the Metropolitan Police, three years after a damning review.
articles.body:
A new report has found institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still exist in the Metropolitan Police, three years after a damning review which urged the force to make significant changes.

The Met has failed to make good progress in all areas flagged as needing improvement.

The landmark report by Dr Gillian Fairfield has been looking at how much the UK's biggest police force has changed since Baroness Louise Casey's scathing review in 2023 .

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he accepted the Fairfield Review's 10 recommendations to help reform the force.

Rowley said he had been "very clear" since he started the job that prejudices including racism, misogyny and homophobia, "have got to be ruthlessly confronted".

Among other criticisms, the Fairfield Review found the Met continued to struggle to acknowledge racism as a structural problem "rather than something people can be trained out of".

It added: "None of these behaviours have changed sufficiently. Neither has the Met's institutional defensiveness."

Fairfield said she was struck by the fact that after a number of strategic briefings with the Met, no senior leader had used the word "racism" and she felt the force was too defensive in its approach.

"Without more bravery than it has shown, the Met cannot fundamentally face its relationship to race and racism," she said.

"If it cannot name it, it cannot face it. The leadership team does not currently do this".

Speaking to BBC Radio London, Fairfield said the Met remains "institutionally very defensive" and "often report things as completed when they're not".

"There is plainly some excellence in the Met," she said.

"The conundrum for the Met is how to make excellence the routine and poor [behaviour] the exception."

The review also raised "serious and worrying criticisms and concerns" about the treatment of bereaved families when the Met carried out investigations into deaths and murders.

Rowley said the report had "some really powerful testimony, some really humbling testimony" from victims affected by the force's handling of their case, and in some instances the Met's actions "made the whole situation worse, not better", which Sir Mark said was "just not acceptable".

What now for the Met? Because the clock is ticking

How many complaints are made against police officers?

The 389-page Fairfield Review, jointly commissioned by the mayor of London and the Met commissioner, examined the progress made by the force after a number of recommendations made in the Casey Review.

It found in some cases the force's "first thought is how the media will react rather than how to fix problems".

Mayor of London Sadiq Khan said the Met must be "fully responsible and accountable for its failings" and "must tackle the culture that allows these behaviours to take root in the first place".

He said a deep-rooted, systemic change was needed to rebuild public trust.

Fairfield also warned further scandals were "highly likely" unless the Met's culture is addressed.

The Casey Review was commissioned after the abduction, rape and murder of Sarah Everard in 2021.

The 33-year-old was walking home in south London when she was taken by police officer Wayne Couzens.

David Carrick, an armed officer in the Met, is currently serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

Another high-profile scandal was later exposed in October 2025 when secret filming at Charing Cross police station by BBC Panorama revealed racism, misogyny and officers boasting about the use of excessive force, as well as jokes about rape and sexual assault.

The Met is also reviewing findings from another BBC Panorama investigation about predatory detective Wayne Arter, who sexually exploited domestic and sexual abuse victims.

His wife Rebekah died in unexplained circumstances in a luxury hotel room in Barbados in June 2024.

Arter took his own life while on remand in July 2024.

The Fairfield Review found some areas of progress including the way misconduct and vetting procedures were handled, as well as some improvements to stop and search transparency powers.

How Met failed to stop rape-unit detective who abused women

Recruitment has also improved - comparing the proportion of ethnic minority workers in the Met from March 2023 to March 2026, there was rise from 15.6% to 19.1% for officers staff and 26% to 30.1% for staff.

These figures are still significantly below London's population, where ethnic minorities make up almost half the population, at 46.3%.

The review also raised concerns about staff reporting bad behaviour.

Less than half (44%) felt confident raising concerns about a senior officer and a quarter said they were "not so confident", while 17% were "not at all" confident their concerns would be acted on.

Around half (49%) of those who felt bullied or harassed at work had not reported it, while of those who had two thirds (67%) said no action had been taken.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has welcomed the Fairfield Review.

"Three years ago, when Baroness Casey completed her report, the force was facing a profound crisis.

"I particularly welcome the improvement in policing serious sexual offences as this government pursues its goal of halving violence against women and girls.

"But there are further improvements required, and I welcome the commissioner's commitment to this".

articles.title: Work starts on Wokingham Council's solar farm to power 9,400 homes
articles.summary: The main construction programme for the 43,000-panel project is due to start in 2027.
articles.body:
Work has started on building a council-owned solar farm that it is hoped will generate enough power for about 9,400 homes.

Wokingham Borough Council said Barkham Solar Farm would provide income to support its services and could be connected to the National Grid from September 2027.

The first phase of enabling work will include creating the site's entrance, establishing its construction compound, and carrying out other preparatory work.

The main construction programme for the 43,000-panel project is due to start next year.

Equans will build the solar farm on council-owned farmland to the north of California Country Park, west of Finchampstead and south of Barkham.

It is expected to generate about 28,500 MWh of electricity every year over 40 years and a surplus of more than £1m annually for the council.

Imogen Shepherd-DuBey, the council's executive member for finance and governance, said the project was "a long-term investment in cleaner energy, the council's financial resilience and the future of the borough".

A greenway is set to run through the site, connecting with a proposed extension to Rook's Nest Wood to the north and California Country Park to its south.

Woodland will be created and the council said it has already worked with the Freely Fruity charity to plant about 1,000 fruit trees at the solar farm site.

West Berkshire Council plans to build its Grazeley Solar Farm, which will produce enough power for about 6,000 homes, from March.

articles.title: Shropshire researchers working to help farmers deal with climate change
articles.summary: Five scientists from Harper Adams University are taking part in a European climate change study.
articles.body:
A team of scientists are working with farmers from across Europe to find solutions to problems caused by climate change.

The researchers in the UK and eight other countries are also looking at how the effects of climate change can be more accurately predicted over the coming century.

Prof Karl Behrendt, who leads a team based at Harper Adams University in Shropshire, said all sorts of adaptation would be considered and it could include diversification into crops not typically seen in the UK.

He also said he hoped a digital tool could be developed for farmers, using artificial intelligence to help advise them and added: "I think what we will come up will be really enlightening."

The ClimAurea project is due to last three years and will explore how changing temperatures, rainfall patterns and extreme events could affect crops, grasslands and livestock across Europe up until the year 2100.

Initially, it is concentrating at the issues faced by farmers in Thessaly, Greece, West Flanders in Belgium, Tara Calatei in Romania and Alentejo in Portugal, but more regions are set to be added.

Behrendt said the four had been chosen because their experience of climate change had been different and they had all adopted different strategies to cope.

He said those strategies could include changes to planting and harvesting times, to irrigation and to the use of fertilisers.

The UK, he said, had already seen farmers moving harvest time because of changing weather.

But at some point, he said farmers might find they "push the limits of what is genetically possible" and at that point it could be worth considering switching to different crops.

Over time, drought and flooding could mean certain crops become less suitable in particular regions, he said.

Behrendt said this was already being seen in the United States with maize.

"30 years ago they wouldn't have thought of growing it anywhere near the Canadian border, but now it's everywhere," he said.

In Europe, he suggested rice was a crop which could be grown more.

There are 63 people working on the ClimAurea project, in 13 teams across nine countries - Luxembourg, UK, Greece, Serbia, France, Italy, Belgium, Romania and Portugal.

One of their aims is to collect enough data to make it possible to predict the effect of climate change on farming over the coming decades.

That information will be used by an interactive digital tool which will be made available to farmers, using AI to offer them advice.

Work started in September, but Behrendt said he had been surprised "how powerful this digital twin will be".

"I've just got this feeling that's going to be quite impactful," he said.

articles.title: Phala Phala farm theft: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
articles.summary: The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
articles.body:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

"It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said.

The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.

The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.

The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.

Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.

The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.

Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.

Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.

The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".

It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".

Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.

He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court , ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.

It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.

In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".

The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.

If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.

If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.

Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.

He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

articles.title: Karthigai Deepam row: Why lighting a lamp has triggered a legal battle in Tamil Nadu
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu government apologised before the Supreme Court on Wednesday after the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp was not lit at the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu government apologised before the Supreme Court on Wednesday after the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp was not lit at the designated Deepathoon stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai on November 24, despite the court's interim direction.In a status report filed by Madurai district collector Nishant Krishna, the state government said the temple's Board of Trustees did not authorise the team proposed to carry out the ritual and instead decided to retain the customary location.The development came after the ceremonial lamp was lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Ucchi Pillayar temple, rather than at Deepathoon, which was the subject of the Supreme Court's November 20 order. The court said it would consider the contempt plea alleging non-compliance with its directions and asked the petitioner and other parties to file appropriate applications.The dispute over the ritual's location has been continuing for years, with Hindu groups seeking permission to light the lamp at the hilltop stone pillar near the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah, while the state government and temple authorities have maintained that the customary venue is near the Ucchi Pillayar temple.Also read| ‘Lamp could not be lit at designated spot’: Tamil Nadu govt apologises in Supreme Court, contempt plea to be heard in Karthigai Deepam rowThe November 24 ceremony, the subsequent explanation by the district administration and the demand for contempt proceedings have now brought the dispute back before the Supreme Court.What is the Karthigai Deepam row?Karthigai Deepam is a traditional Tamil Hindu festival celebrated by lighting lamps in homes and temples. At Thiruparankundram, the dispute concerns the location where the ceremonial lamp, or Maha Deepam, should be lit during the annual festival.For decades, the lamp has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple on the lower slopes of Thiruparankundram hill. However, Hindu groups have sought permission to light it at Deepathoon, a stone pillar located higher up the hill and around 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah.The disagreement is not limited to the ritual's location. It also involves competing claims over the stone pillar's character and the hilltop's ownership and status. While Hindu groups describe Deepathoon as an ancient structure associated with the ritual, another side argues that it is a survey stone. The dargah committee has also contested the demand, claiming ownership of the hilltop.The dispute has travelled through the courts over several years. In December 2025, a single judge of the Madras High Court directed the temple authorities to light the lamp at Deepathoon. A division bench upheld the direction in its January 6, 2026, judgment. The state government subsequently challenged the High Court's decision before the Supreme Court.The Tamil Nadu government and the temple administration have maintained that the lamp has traditionally been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple. The state has also raised concerns over the legal and administrative implications of allowing the ritual at the disputed pillar, including the possibility of law-and-order complications because of its proximity to the dargah.What did the Supreme Court order on November 20On November 20, a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi permitted the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam lamp at Deepathoon on November 24 as a one-time interim arrangement. The order came while the Supreme Court was hearing challenges to the Madras High Court's directions on the ritual.The court allowed only a restricted team authorised by the temple administration and government officials to go to the location and carry out the ceremony. It also designated the district collector as the nodal officer responsible for coordination and supervision.The Supreme Court imposed safeguards to prevent any escalation at the disputed site. It restrained members of the public from going to the location and prohibited processions, public gatherings, slogan-raising and demonstrations during the ceremony. The court also stayed portions of the Madras High Court judgment that had upheld the direction to restore the practice of lighting the lamp at Deepathoon.Importantly, the permission was limited to November 24 and did not settle the larger dispute over the ritual's history, the hilltop's ownership, or any customary or religious right to light the lamp at the pillar. The court clarified that neither the permission nor the ceremony could be treated as proof of an established custom or a continuing right of access to the location.The Tamil Nadu government subsequently approached the Supreme Court seeking a review of the November 20 order and a stay on the one-time permission. However, the interim direction remained the basis for the November 24 arrangements.What happened on November 24The Karthigai Deepam ceremony took place amid heightened security and tension at Thiruparankundram on November 24. However, the lamp was not lit at Deepathoon, the location specified by the Supreme Court. Instead, the Maha Deepam was lit at the customary Deepa Mandapam near the Ucchi Pillayar temple at around 6 pm.The development came hours after Madurai collector Nishant Krishna told the Madurai bench of the Madras High Court that the Supreme Court's directions would be implemented. The High Court had also reminded officials of their responsibility to comply with the apex court's order and warned of contempt proceedings in the event of non-compliance.State law minister C T R Nirmalkumar confirmed the lighting at the customary location in a post on X, saying: "Karthigai Mahadeepam has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam near Ucchi Pillaiyar temple, directly above the sanctum sanctorum of the presiding deity at Thiruparankundram".The decision triggered protests by Hindu organisations and BJP workers, who demanded that the government implement the Supreme Court's direction. Tensions were reported near the hill, where protesters raised slogans against the state government. Police had deployed more than 5,600 personnel in Thiruparankundram and adjoining areas, with restrictions imposed on public access to the hilltop.The district administration later said that the last-minute decision to retain the customary venue followed concerns raised by the temple's Board of Trustees. The trustees maintained that the Deepa Mandapam was the traditional location for the ritual and that the practice should continue there.Why did the Madurai collector say the lamp could not be lit at DeepathoonIn a status report filed before the Supreme Court, Madurai district collector Nishant Krishna said the administration had made arrangements to implement the November 20 order but could not proceed because the temple's Board of Trustees did not authorise the team proposed to light the lamp.According to the district administration's explanation, the Supreme Court had designated the collector as the coordinating officer, while the temple administration was responsible for authorising the personnel who would carry out the ritual. The administration said it had completed the necessary arrangements, but the trustees eventually resolved to retain the customary location.The Board of Trustees cited religious traditions and established worship practices in support of its decision. It maintained that the Deepa Mandapam near the Ucchi Pillayar temple was the customary venue and that the location was directly above the head of Lord Murugan, the presiding deity. The trustees also referred to Agama rules governing temple rituals and festivals.In its statement after the ceremony, the district administration said: "The trustees unanimously resolved to retain the customary venue, citing religious traditions and established worship practices."The trustees said their decision followed an examination of historical and religious records and consultations with the temple's Sthanikars, or hereditary ritual functionaries. They also decided to place their findings before the court.The collector apologised for the failure to light the lamp at Deepathoon and maintained that the administration had made every effort to comply with the Supreme Court's direction. The state's position was that the district administration could not independently authorise another team to perform the ritual in the absence of the temple Board of Trustees' approval.The status report also maintained that there had been no wilful or deliberate disobedience of the Supreme Court's directions. The government said the failure to carry out the ceremony at the designated location was due to the trustees' decision to retain the customary venue.What is the contempt plea against Tamil Nadu officialsThe failure to light the lamp at Deepathoon led to demands for contempt proceedings against the state authorities. The petitioner seeking permission for the ritual alleged that the government had failed to comply with the Supreme Court's November 20 direction despite assurances given before the Madras High Court that the order would be implemented.During Wednesday's proceedings, a senior advocate appearing for the petitioner termed the developments "most unfortunate". He argued that the flame should have been carried to Deepathoon and the lamp lit there, and alleged deliberate non-compliance with the apex court's directions.The counsel also urged the Supreme Court to initiate suo motu contempt proceedings against the authorities concerned. When the senior advocate indicated that the petitioners would move a contempt plea, the bench said, "File it, and then we will see."The Supreme Court asked the petitioner and other parties to file appropriate applications and said it would hear the matter. The bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi also said it would peruse the status report filed by the state government.The contempt allegation centres on whether the authorities failed to implement the Supreme Court's specific direction despite the district administration being tasked with coordinating the ceremony. The state government, however, has denied wilful disobedience and attributed the failure to the temple trustees' decision not to authorise the proposed team.The Supreme Court's consideration of the contempt plea will therefore bring the conduct of the officials and the explanation submitted by the district administration under judicial scrutiny.Opposition slams Tamil Nadu governmentThe failure to light the lamp at Deepathoon has triggered sharp criticism from BJP leaders, who have accused the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government of disregarding the Supreme Court's interim order and hurting the sentiments of devotees.BJP national general secretary B L Santhosh accused the state government of defying the court's directions and said the government would face a "civilisational and legal challenge". In a post on X, he alleged that the Madurai district administration had lit the lamp at the Ucchi Pillayar Mandapam instead of the Deepathoon stone pillar as directed by the Supreme Court.Also read| ‘Crores of devotees let down’: BJP slams Vijay govt for defying SC order on Deepam rowIn another post, Santhosh accused the government of compromising the sentiments of devotees to accommodate its political allies. He said: "You people have hurt devotes & defied SC Order to please some alliance partners & you yourself is Law Minister of a Govt which will fully defied SC Order . To please some friends you let down crores of devotees," he alleged.Tamil Nadu BJP president Nainar Nagenthran also accused the state government and district administration of failing to implement the court's order. He criticised the decision to light the lamp at the customary location after the collector had assured the Madras High Court that the Supreme Court's direction would be followed."Lighting the lamp at the Pillaiyar temple after assuring the court that arrangements were being made is an act of deception. It is akin to fooling a child with candy, and they are attempting to deceive the Supreme Court and High Court judges," Nagenthran said.BJP leader Tamilisai Soundararajan also accused the government of violating the interim order and alleged that the decision was taken to appease its alliance partners. She questioned why the government had not raised its objections based on Agama rules before the Supreme Court.The BJP's criticism came alongside protests by Hindu organisations in different parts of Tamil Nadu. Demonstrations were reported in Ramanathapuram and Pollachi, where protesters demanded that the government comply with the Supreme Court's direction. Police detained protesters involved in road blockades, while cases were registered against members of BJP and Hindu organisations over the demonstrations.The state government and temple trustees, however, have defended the decision to retain the customary location, citing religious traditions and established worship practices.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jungle announced as first Latitude Festival headliner
articles.summary: Founder and director Melvin Benn says the 2027 festival will be "bolder than anything we've done".
articles.body:
Brit Award winning soul band Jungle are the first to be announced as headliners for the 2027 Latitude Festival.

The festival, which is back for its 21st year, will take place from 22 to 25 July at Henham Park, near Southwold in Suffolk.

Jungle's headline slot has been described as a "full circle moment" after the band, known for hits including Back on 74 and Volcano, made their Latitude debut in 2014.

Founder and festival director, Melvin Benn, said the 2027 festival would be "bolder than anything we've done".

Two further headliners are yet to be announced.

A full programme of comedy, theatre, literature, poetry, dance and the arts is also due to be revealed.

Benn said: "Latitude has always been about what comes next, and 2027 will be bolder than anything we've done.

"Part of that is backing artists early and bringing them back bigger. Jungle played the Second Stage here in 2014. Now they headline.

"That's what Latitude is about: giving artists the platform to take the next step, and welcoming them back as they reach new heights."

He said the festival was "continuing to push its boundaries and create something that feels distinctive, ambitious and full of surprises".

articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose deportation sparked legal battle for Trump admin, leaves US for Spain voluntarily
articles.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador by the Trump administration despite a court order protecting him
articles.body: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who was mistakenly deported to El Salvador by the Trump administration despite a court order protecting him from removal, has voluntarily left the United States for Spain, his lawyers and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed on Tuesday. His deportation in March 2025 had triggered a major legal battle and drawn widespread criticism of the administration's immigration crackdown.The 31-year-old reached an agreement with federal authorities to leave the US voluntarily rather than face another forced deportation. CNN reported that Garcia travelled to Spain on a commercial flight along with his American wife and attorney.The advocacy group We Are CASA, which has supported Garcia and his family, also confirmed his departure, saying he had "walked out of the United States a free man". According to the organisation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents removed his ankle monitor at the airport.Garcia is now expected to undertake international speaking engagements in several countries.Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who had campaigned for Garcia's release and met him at a prison in El Salvador last year, welcomed the development."A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag. Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity," Van Hollen said in a statement.How Garcia became the face of Trump's deportation crackdownGarcia's case became a major flashpoint in the Trump administration's immigration crackdown after he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite an immigration judge's earlier order preventing his removal to the country.He had entered the US illegally as a teenager around 2011 and had been living in Maryland with his American wife and child. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because a gang there had threatened him and his family.Although he was allowed to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, he was not granted permanent residency.Despite the protection order, US authorities arrested Garcia in Baltimore and deported him to El Salvador, where he was detained at Cecot, a notorious mega-prison. The Trump administration subsequently acknowledged in court documents that his deportation had happened because of an administrative error.A federal judge ordered the government to work towards bringing him back to the US, but the administration resisted for months. Garcia was eventually returned to American soil in June 2025 after the US reached an arrangement with El Salvador.However, his return was followed by another legal battle. He was arrested on human-smuggling charges in Tennessee, but a federal judge dismissed the case in May 2026, citing what was described as a "tainted investigation". The Justice Department has appealed the ruling.Trump administration wanted to deport him to African countriesEven after Garcia returned to the US, the Trump administration continued pursuing his removal, proposing several African countries as possible destinations.Officials had considered Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia for his deportation. Garcia had previously expressed a preference for Costa Rica, which had indicated it could offer him some form of legal status.However, conditions imposed by the federal judge who dismissed his criminal case prevented him from voluntarily travelling there.According to CNN, the administration continued its efforts to arrange third-country deportations even as Garcia challenged his removal in court. The dispute took another turn in October, when a scheduled court hearing on his possible deportation to Liberia was abruptly cancelled after lawyers for both sides left the courtroom with Garcia.The latest agreement allows him to leave the US voluntarily for Spain, avoiding another forced removal.Van Hollen said he was relieved that Garcia would be able to live in a country of his choice and remain free from what he described as the administration's constant persecution.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ethan Ives-Griffiths murder: Missed chances to save boy killed by grandparents
articles.summary: Safeguarding board apologises "unreservedly" after a review into the death of the Flintshire toddler.
articles.body:
Opportunities to protect a two-year-old who was murdered by his grandparents were missed by multiple agencies, a review has found.

Ethan Ives-Griffiths died on 16 August 2021 after suffering a "catastrophic" head injury at his grandparents' home in Garden City, Flintshire. He had been beaten, starved and deprived of fluids.

North Wales Safeguarding Board apologised "unreservedly" after a review found attempts by his dad to raise concerns were not acted upon.

Michael Ives, 49, and Kerry Ives, 47, were jailed for life in 2025 . Ethan's mum, Shannon Ives, 29, was jailed for 12 years for causing or allowing his death and child cruelty.

Flintshire council said it "failed" Ethan and was "deeply sorry".

Warning: This article contains details of violence and abuse that some may find distressing

When Ethan died, he was dangerously dehydrated and severely underweight, with 40 visible bruises or marks.

After his grandparents were found guilty, Mr Justice Griffiths said the pair had engaged in a "campaign to break him" and text messages from Michael Ives said the toddler would have to "learn the hard way".

Ethan was "a shadow of the chubby healthy child he had been" in the days before he fatally collapsed, the judge said.

Co-chair of the safeguarding board, Nicola Stubbins, said the child practice review, published on Wednesday, made "difficult reading".

She said: "We apologise unreservedly that those multi-agency systems did not protect Ethan as they should have.

"We owe it to Ethan to ensure that the vital lessons from this case lead to lasting changes in our professional practice."

The Ives family was well known to health and education services, Flintshire Council's children's services, and North Wales police, because of issues surrounding "significant domestic violence", substance abuse and homelessness - with 36 referrals and concerns raised about Ethan or his immediate family since 2016.

The review, which refers to Ethan as Child E, noted a history of "non-engagement" with services by Ethan's mother and her family, but found there was "no escalation of concern", with a high proportion of cases closed with no further action.

It also found wider communication between agencies was impacted by IT systems which did not share all the historical information held on file regarding previous referrals.

When his mother and father, Will Griffiths, split on 9 June 2021, police in attendance noted that Ethan's father was "begging" the social worker not to take him to his grandparents, but there was no record that was shared with the children's service.

The family were initially sent to Shannon's sister, where staff thought Ethan would be safe, but later - unbeknown to the council - went to live in the home of Michael and Kerry Ives, in Garden City.

At the time, the review noted school staff, the social worker and the police officer involved thought they were instrumental in sending the children to safety, "little did they know this was the first step in [Ethan's] demise".

The "impact of this knowledge continues to be felt by these staff, who have noted the lack of support they have felt from their respective agencies since this time", the report added.

When Shannon Ives informed children's services on 7 July that Ethan was living with his grandparents, there was no record of any checks being made about his welfare and his address was not changed on the IT system, the review found.

Griffiths told reviewers he had contacted the council to express concerns about Ethan's mother and her parents, but "no one listened".

The report states it was "well documented" that there were concerns about Ethan's grandparents' care and highlighted a "missed opportunity" by Flintshire children's services to "gain valuable information".

Though national guidelines set out in Wales Safeguarding Procedures state that children on the child protection register should been seen by social workers every 10 days, the last time Ethan was seen was 22 July 2021 - more than three weeks before his death - despite a number of attempted home visits.

During a visit on 5 August, a social worker waited on the doorstep for 45 minutes, but did not see Ethan because Shannon and Kerry Ives said he was asleep. CCTV footage later revealed Ethan had already been a victim of physical abuse at this point, which his mother and grandmother were attempting to conceal.

Several attempts to see the children by a social worker and health visitor occurred over subsequent days, but access was denied each time.

The review also considered the effect of the Covid19 pandemic on the provision of social services - with social workers having to isolate and some agency workers brought in from outside the local authority area.

It noted an "unprecedented increase" in referrals by 76 per cent in the three months between March 2021 and June 2021 had also placed an "additional significant pressure" on services.

However, the review concluded a repeated feature of the case was the "missed opportunities" by the various agencies to hear the voices of the Ives children, especially Ethan.

It said there was little information about him in reports and discussions, and files did not "capture his needs, his character, his likes or dislikes".

In one police report, which recorded the events of 9 June 2021 - when Shannon Ives and her children were moved from their family home, there was no mention of him, despite being present.

"From the information shared," reads the report, "it is safe to say that [Ethan's] voice was not heard."

The report set out 16 recommendations to "strengthen safeguarding practice across agencies" with Fôn Roberts, chair of the review, stating Ethan must remain "at the centre".

"He was a young boy who needed safety, care and protection," he said.

"His voice was not heard, and historical information was not consistently brought together."

He stressed new policies, training and systems "must translate into consistent practice".

"The priority must be to embed the learning and demonstrate that it makes a meaningful difference to the safety and wellbeing of children," Roberts said.

In a statement, Flintshire County Council said the "profound impact" of Ethan's death had left a "lasting effect on the professionals and teams responsible for safeguarding children in Flintshire".

It said the child practice review "highlighted areas where information recording and sharing, professional curiosity and co-ordinated intervention could have, and should have, been stronger".

The council apologised to Ethan's father and said it would work to strengthen its approach to "engaging with fathers and male carers in our work with families".

"We recognise that our services were part of the safeguarding response and accept our responsibility for the shortcomings identified by the review.

"We are deeply sorry for the areas where we failed Ethan."

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
articles.summary: The BBC's technology and AI editor on how Nvidia's boss made himself impossible to fire.
articles.body:
Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned . Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X .

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).

In addition, Huang has powerful allies, and they are mostly powerful men. US President Donald Trump personally pushed for his return to Nvidia, while Elon Musk said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

He is one of very few people who knows both Trump and China's President Xi Jinping personally - and somehow he has surfed the geopolitical tension between the two continents.

He has said he thinks both China and the US can win the AI race and called on them to pull together.

And finally there's the bottom line, which is always money.

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns

Huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again.

It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff.

Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the company they work for as part of their pay packages.

Nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life.

With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

articles.title: Psychology says children who are praised for being intelligent rather than hardworking may develop a surprising fear of failure
articles.summary: When a child scores well on a test or when they perform a task that they couldn’t perform before, adults naturally give compliments about their
articles.body: When a child scores well on a test or when they perform a task that they couldn’t perform before, adults naturally give compliments about their intelligence. A child solves a difficult maths problem, and the immediate response is, "You are so intelligent!" A room full of adults would automatically discuss how gifted the child is when they score good grades. While these compliments come from a place of love, psychology suggests that they may carry the message that being smart is important which leaves less room for making mistakes.It sounds harmless, doesn't it? After all, what parent would not want their child to feel intelligent and capable? However, researchers have found that children who get praised for their intelligence tend to become more concerned about this image of being clever. They are unable to enjoy the process of learning something new and just become obsessed to fetch compliments about their intelligence. When their efforts are not recognised after success, they become less inclined to work harder when they eventually face failure, as everyone inevitably does.The psychology behind praising intelligenceA 1998 study titled ‘Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance’ explored how different kinds of praise influence children’s motivation after success and failure. The researchers conducted six experiments involving fifth-grade students. After successfully completing a task, while some students were praised for their intelligence, others were praised for their effort. The interesting findings came out when these students were made to go through failure in the next step.It was noticed that the children who had been praised for their intelligence after success showed less persistence. They enjoyed the difficult task less and even performed worse afterwards. Due to lack of acknowledgement for their efforts, they were also more prone to interpreting their poor performance as evidence that they lacked ability.On the other hand, children praised for their effort understood that while the end result matters, their attempts at performing the task mean much more. It was observed that these kids were more willing to continue trying and showed greater interest in learning from the challenging task.When being smart becomes a burdenImagine two children preparing for an examination. Both receive excellent marks, both recieve praise from their parents, but the content of praise differs.While the first child is complimented with, "You are naturally brilliant. You always get everything right!" While the second child is praised with, "You worked hard, practised regularly and found a good way to solve those difficult questions."While initially, both children would feel equally happy. But over time, the messages they receive may shape how they approach difficulties.For the first child, their success would get associated with being intelligent and a poor grade in future would not just be an academic setback. It would feel like they have lost the ability to be smart. This can lead to drastic effects like they might avoid difficult subjects, hesitate to ask questions or refuse to attempt something new. This would be because they would fear what others would think. They would not want others to discover that they do not know everything.The second child, on the other hand, has been encouraged to recognise the value of practice and learning. They have learnt that a mistake does not necessarily mean they are not intelligent; it simply means there is something they have yet to understand.This is closely connected to what psychologists call a fixed mindset and a growth mindset. A fixed mindset views intelligence and abilities as relatively unchangeable, while a growth mindset recognises that skills and knowledge can develop through learning, effective strategies and sustained effort.Why children may start avoiding challengesWhen the focus remains on praise related to a child's intelligence, children start associating learning with performance. Instead of measuring learning outcomes with questions like, "What can I learn from this?", children may start thinking, "What if I get this wrong?" The children focus on protecting their reputation of being clever and forget about actually understanding a subject.This can lead to consequences for a child’s regular learning process at school and at home. They might fear asking the wrong questions which can restrict them from participating in class. The child may not be willing to learn new skills because of the fear of failure. This affects a child's overall growth and development.A 2018 study titled 'Effects of Ability and Effort Praise on Children's Failure Attribution, Self-Handicapping, and Performance', examined how different forms of praise affected fifth-grade students. The findings suggested that children praised for their abilities were more likely to use defensive strategies when faced with failure, including self-handicapping. This can hinder their subsequent improvement. Therefore, in such situations, the focus becomes not on improving but on appearing smart.What should parents praise instead?The research does not suggest that parents should stop calling their children intelligent or celebrate their achievements. However, it is important to ensure that along with intelligence, the efforts put behind their success are recognised. They should understand that while good results are important, failure does not take away their hardwork from them.Parents can simply make small, meaningful changes in the language they use. Instead of saying, "You are so smart", they can say, "I liked how patiently you worked through that problem." Rather than focusing only on good marks, they can appreciate the preparation, curiosity and strategies that helped the child improve.Moreover, it is important to normalise making mistakes. A mistake should not feel like a crime to a child, instead, they should be seen as an opportunity to improve. Parents should avoid fixing everything that a child does wrong, they should instead provide space for discussion. Questions about what they found challenging and how the child would approach the problem if given another chance can make failure feel less frightening.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Rohingya genocide:  What ICJ's historic ruling really means for Myanmar & its refugees
articles.summary: In a historic first, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) recently held Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against its Rohingya minority
articles.body: In a historic first, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) recently held Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against its Rohingya minority during the military's brutal 2017 crackdown. The November 19 judgment marked an extraordinary moment in international law as the world's highest court had never before held a state responsible for carrying out a genocide.The ruling moved the Rohingya's suffering beyond allegations and condemnation to a formal finding of state responsibility for one of the gravest crimes known to humanity. The verdict also struck a major blow to the military establishment that has ruled Myanmar with impunity, adding to the international pressure on its leadership, already isolated and facing sanctions since the 2021 coup that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's civilian government.But the significance of this judgment extends far beyond its legal precedent.Can a landmark verdict translate into justice on the ground? For the Rohingya, that means accountability for those responsible, recognition of the atrocities they endured and, above all, the possibility of returning home safely after hundreds of thousands were driven into exile. For Myanmar, it could become a defining test of whether a state held guilty of genocide can ever be compelled to confront its crimes and change course.The ICJ rulingThe case dates back to 2019, when the Muslim-majority West African nation of The Gambia, approached the ICJ, accusing Myanmar of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.Under the convention, the court had to determine whether Naypyidaw had acted with the specific intent to "destroy, in whole or in part", the Rohingya as a group — the legal threshold for establishing genocide.In its November 19 judgment, the 15-member ICJ bench ruled by a 9-6 majority that Myanmar was responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya, rejecting Naypyidaw’s defence that the 2017 military campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.The court also found that Myanmar's security forces had perpetrated widespread sexual violence, committed acts of extreme violence against children and attacked Rohingya fleeing across the border into Bangladesh.Sreeparna Banerjee, a Myanmar expert at the Observer Research Foundation, described the verdict as a significant legal and political setback for the state.“The ruling reinforces the state's obligation to prevent genocide, protect the Rohingya and ensure accountability. It also strengthens the international recognition of the Rohingya's suffering and places Myanmar under greater legal and diplomatic scrutiny,” she told The Times of India.Yet, while the judgment is final and legally binding, with no right of appeal, the ICJ has no direct enforcement mechanism. This leaves its implementation uncertain, particularly as Naypyidaw has, unsurprisingly, rejected the ruling.What it means for Myanmar's military juntaFor years, Myanmar maintained that the 2017 military operations were a response to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, a Rohingya insurgent group operating in Rakhine state, where the crisis unfolded. With the state now formally held responsible for genocide, that justification has been fundamentally undermined, marking a major challenge to Naypyidaw's long-standing account of the military crackdown.However, the ICJ's finding of state responsibility does not establish the individual criminal liability of military commanders or political leaders. Determining who within the military chain of command should face prosecution remains a separate legal process.This distinction is particularly significant for President Min Aung Hlaing, who was Myanmar's military chief during the 2017 Rohingya crackdown and later led the coup that ousted the civilian government.The judgment could nevertheless have far-reaching implications for Myanmar's military leadership.“The ruling increases international scrutiny of the military leadership and weakens its attempts to normalise its international standing. It could reinforce broader efforts to pursue accountability and further constrain the junta's diplomatic legitimacy,” Banerjee said.The ICJ has also directed Naypyidaw to investigate those suspected of committing acts of genocide and prosecute and punish them where warranted. This places the military establishment in a difficult position as it is now under a legal obligation to pursue accountability for atrocities committed by its own security forces, raising serious questions about whether it would be willing to investigate and prosecute those within its own ranks.The challenge of ensuring accountabilityWith the ICJ lacking an enforcement mechanism and Myanmar's military leadership unlikely to hold its own ranks accountable, the challenge of establishing individual responsibility remains.One possible route to enforcing the judgment lies in Article 94 of the UN Charter, should The Gambia, which brought the case before the ICJ, choose to invoke the provision.Under Article 94(1), UN member states are obligated to comply with ICJ judgments in cases to which they are parties. If a state fails to do so, the other party may approach the UN Security Council under Article 94(2). The Council may then make recommendations or decide on measures to give effect to the judgment.However, whether this can lead to meaningful action is also uncertain. Of the five permanent members of the Security Council, China and Russia maintain active diplomatic ties with Myanmar, while the United Kingdom and France have welcomed the ICJ ruling. The fifth, the United States, has responded more cautiously, saying it was reviewing the judgment while reiterating its support for the people of Myanmar.Washington's response is perhaps unsurprising. Although the US continues to impose sanctions on Myanmar, the Trump administration recently held direct talks with the country’s military leadership, suggesting a possible shift in its approach towards the junta.Banerjee agreed that enforcing the judgment would be difficult and would, to a large extent, depend on Myanmar's own political will to comply. "Enforcement remains difficult … implementation depends largely on Myanmar's compliance, international pressure and, in certain circumstances, the UN Security Council, where geopolitical divisions could complicate action," she added.Rohingya repatriationThe scale of the Rohingya crisis is immense. Before the 2017 crackdown, around 1.1 million Rohingya were living in Myanmar, mainly in Rakhine state.According to an independent UN fact-finding mission, more than 740,000 have since fled to neighbouring Bangladesh, joining earlier waves of refugees and bringing the Rohingya population there to around 1.2 million.Today, only around 600,000 Rohingya remain in Rakhine, including 140,000 living in displacement camps.For Rohingya refugees, therefore, the more immediate question is whether the ruling can help secure the conditions needed for their safe and voluntary return to Myanmar, particularly as the ICJ has also directed the state to ensure the safe and voluntary return of those who fled or were displaced, and to provide financial compensation to the victims.However, the judgment does not set an immediate timeline for repatriation. Nor can a legal order by itself create the conditions necessary for refugees to return. The continuing conflict in Rakhine state, the absence of security guarantees and the Rohingya’s longstanding exclusion from Myanmar’s political and social life remain major obstacles.As a result, the prospects of a return home remain extremely limited.“Repatriation will depend on conditions on the ground, including security, citizenship, freedom of movement and guarantees against persecution. Without these, meaningful repatriation remains unlikely in the near term,” Banerjee noted.The verdict may have brought some measure of closure to the victims by holding Myanmar legally responsible for the genocide. But for the Rohingya, justice will remain incomplete until they can return home safely — a prospect that remains unlikely, at least in the foreseeable future.Political implications for MyanmarThe ICJ ruling came just days before Asean, the Southeast Asian bloc of which Myanmar is a member, extended its exclusion of the country's military leadership, including Min Aung Hlaing, from participating in its high-level political meetings.The ban was imposed and extended following periodic reviews over Naypyidaw’s failure to implement the Five-Point Consensus agreed with Asean in 2021. The framework aimed at addressing Myanmar’s political and humanitarian crisis following the military coup.For the Rohingya, the post-coup crisis has further compounded their suffering. A UN report in August described them as facing "systematic discrimination by all parties, with absolute impunity", referring to both Myanmar’s military government and the Arakan Army, which now controls almost 90% of Rakhine state.Therefore, for a state seeking international legitimacy, starting with its immediate neighbourhood, the ruling comes as further diplomatic setback.However, its domestic impact is likely to remain limited. “The ruling could become an important reference point in discussions on Myanmar's future political settlement, particularly concerning accountability, minority rights and inclusive governance. However, amid the ongoing conflict and fragmented political landscape, its immediate influence on the country's political trajectory is likely to remain limited,” said Banerjee.The road ahead for the RohingyaThe ICJ judgment represents a significant milestone in the Rohingya’s quest for justice, but it does not resolve the political and humanitarian crisis that continues to affect them. It has established Myanmar's responsibility and outlined what the state must do to address the consequences of its actions.The challenge now is to ensure that these obligations are fulfilled.The coming months will be important in determining whether the verdict leads to sustained international pressure, progress towards accountability and concrete steps towards repatriation. Much will depend on Naypyidaw’s own willingness, the response of major powers, and the ability of the international community to maintain pressure on Myanmar.The ruling is an important recognition of the Rohingya’s suffering. But its real significance will ultimately be measured not only by the legal precedent it sets, but by whether it changes the conditions in which they live and makes a safe return to their homeland possible.You use AI every day.
